utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances first?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with my learned colleagues, Mr. Giuliano Turone, Ms. Teresa McHenry and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten, our case manager. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And the defence. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. This morning the defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic consists of Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo, and Eugene O'Sullivan, criminal law professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Michael Greaves. I appear on behalf of the defendant Mucic and I am assisted today by my learned friend Ms. Mira Tapuskovic. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honour, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. Together with me in the team is Mr. Tom Moran from Houston, Texas. We are defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. MR. BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am the attorney Mustafa Brackovic from Sarajevo. Together with me in the defence of Esad Landzo is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey, attorney from Houston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now we have a motion this morning which concerns the admissibility of extra judicial statements made by accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think on 17th January when it was discussed at a status conference I made it clear it was not ripe for consideration of such matters and it should be discussed at a time when the statement comes to be determined and I notice that it appears.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. There seems to be no interpretation. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I apologise, your Honours. I get no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there anything going through now? Still no interpretation? I hear the equipment is working now; is that right? So we will begin again. At the beginning I said we have before us a motion this morning on the consideration of extra judicial statements of accused persons. When it was first discussed on 17th January I indicated at that time that the time was not ripe for consideration of such evidence and the time should be when the statement is distributed. I still find that there have been -- the motion is still tabled and I would now like to hear exactly why we should consider it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Yesterday morning I raised the question whether we should postpone hearing it. We are, from the side of the prosecution, in no hurry. On the other hand, with respect to the witness on our last witness list we submitted to the court, and to the defence, we would request the court to at least postpone the hearing on this motion until we have finished this witness, who is now under cross-examination, and another three waiting in our witness room to be examined. So for me it is -- I would prefer a decision from the court considering this thing to be postponed until a convenient time in two weeks or something like that. We do not even have, in my opinion, to set a fixed date for it today. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So what is the view on the part of the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is this: there plainly has to be a decision before these statements are introduced as evidence, and the point of making the objection at this stage was the prosecution have indicated they wanted to have those statements introduced fairly soon, and when I filed my -- was preparing my motion in the week we had away from court, I anticipated it was going to be fairly soon after that. The second point is this: the final part of my motion is this, that the introduction of the statements halfway through the eyewitness evidence is an inappropriate time for it to be done, so a decision has to be reached as to when those statements should be adduced as evidence, at the end of the prosecution case or in the middle of it. So I am afraid the time has come when a decision has to be made. Whether that should be today or should be put off, as my learned friend, Mr. Ostberg, has indicated, for sound practical reasons is, of course, a matter for your Honours and I do not necessarily dissent from that, knowing it is an important decision and we are aware of other obvious difficulties as well that obtain. So I think that is our view, that we have got to make a decision at some stage before those statements come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think your strategy is one of an anticipatory decision of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One always likes to deal with difficulties before they have arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now there are certain hurdles which you do not try to jump before you get to the time. Here, if your argument is the question of whether it is admissible at all, my memory is that has been decided and that it did not conflict with any of the provisions of the Rules by the Trial Chamber itself. So I do not know exactly the basis for the argument now, except my memory does not serve me right, but I think the prosecution should be able to -- or any of you who was involved in that argument should be able to testify whether such a decision has been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know of no such decision, but, of course, your Honour will recall that I arrived slightly later than others in these proceedings. Be that as it may, if a decision has been made, I invite this Tribunal to reopen it, because it is an important matter, and important matters are raised absolutely fundamental to the fairness of this case. If a decision has not been made on this matter, then plainly you can now proceed to decide upon it. I invite the court to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear from others whether such a decision has been taken. If not, we agree with you. It is fundamental. Admissibility is a serious matter. So if it has not been decided, we can go ahead and do that, but if it has been, I do not think we will invite it. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, by the submission of the defence counsel for Mr. Delalic, to exclude the evidence gathered in Munich in the provisions from these motions can be discussed at a time when the Prosecutor decides to adduce this evidence during the presentation of evidence. In the status conference in January we again reopened this issue, because the decision of the Trial Chamber intimated that this should be discussed at a time when this evidence is presented, and on the list of witnesses from December this was -- this also included those that were pursuant to Rules 42 and 43. At that point you indicated that it was premature to discuss the admissibility of this evidence and that we should discuss this at a time when the Prosecutor decides which witness statements they will decide to present. The Prosecutor has also submitted in writing that they intend to use this in evidence, and I completely concur with my learned colleague that this issue and this motion should be decided upon, and to take a decision on whether this evidence is admissible or not. However, I fully agree that this need not be done now. We did have a discussion on this yesterday with Mr. Ostberg, and we are in agreement that we can revisit this issue in about ten, fifteen days after several witnesses who have been waiting will have been questioned. But I urge the Trial Chamber to take such a decision, which has not been taken so far, and that this should be done in the next ten to fifteen days so that the defence would know clearly whether the whole statements made by our clients are admissible before this Trial Chamber. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If I might, just on the part of Esad Landzo, your Honour, I am not sure that it is clear to Mr. Greaves, and it is not clear to me, so I am asking for -- there are two separate issues on admissibility that we have before the court at this point, and the two separate issues are the admissibility or the legality of the seizure of the evidence with regard to the defendants Delalic and Mucic, which Esad Landzo has no standing to challenge, and then the second issue is the admissibility of the co-defendants' statements as against each other. I am not clear which one we are dealing with at this moment, because they are both before the court at this time. If it is the admissibility of the co-defendants' statements as against each other, then each one of us believes that fundamental rights of the accused will be affected, and that does need to be decided before the prosecution decides to use any statements secured from any of the accused, but if it has to do with the seizure of the material in Munich or in Vienna, then, of course, that is a different matter completely. So I am asking for clarification of which issue of admissibility we are dealing with at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually in the main the court avoids dealing with accidental or hypothetical questions. The issue of co-accuseds' statements has not arisen. We do not know whether it will be introduced or not. Nobody ever talks about it at this stage. We are more interested in the admissibility of the statements of accused persons when they were interviewed, not now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I can and maybe I cannot try to clarify what is happening. The prosecution intends in the very near future to introduce the statements of the accused when they were interviewed into evidence, and we intend to do that after Witness I, which is, I believe, three witnesses away. In anticipation of some of the legal issues that we believed would be raised by those and which defence counsel had raised in some of their motions, we filed the response, so -- just to give the court advance consideration of some of the issues. As Mr. Ostberg has said, it is our -- and as I hear your Honour to say also -- it is our belief that those issues can be appropriately handled when, in fact, we introduce the witness who is going to raise those. So we had not been seeking an anticipatory Ruling, but we were just trying to give both the defence and the Chamber some advance notice of our position on the legal issues. We do anticipate having a witness in a couple of days. With respect to the prior decisions that have been made or not made, let me just address that for one minute. The rules of this Tribunal state that among the preliminary motions which the accused must bring within 60 days, or in any event prior to trial, are motions to exclude evidence, which would include interviews. In this case, none of the accused, except for Mr. Delalic, have made such a motion, and, as I understand, both from that and from their written submissions there, in fact, is not an argument that the statements are not admissible against the accused themselves. The issue is whether or not the evidence could be considered against co-accused. It is the case with respect to Mr. -- and this is, in fact, applicable to both the seizure of evidence and the statements, but for now I will just talk about statements -- it is the case that when Mr. Delalic initially raised his motion to exclude both the evidence and the statements, the Trial Chamber dealt with all the legal issues and rejected them and said they were not grounds. There was one technical issue, which the court said it would reserve ruling on until such time as they were introduced, and I believe that is still outstanding, and the prosecution agrees that that particular issue with respect to the first interview of Mr. Delalic will still be outstanding, but other than that, as I understand -- so, to summarise, in about three or four witnesses, within the next several weeks, we intend to introduce the statements of all the accused. With respect to the first interview of Mr. Delalic, there is an issue about whether or not the technical recording requirements were met. That issue has not been decided. With respect to the other, I think, arguments of the accused, as I understand it, the argument is only -- relates to whether or not this evidence may be used against the co-accused, which is, in fact, something that we are not going to be asking the court to rule on even then, but that is sort of the issue raised. I do not know if that has been helpful or confusing, but that is my summary of the prior Rulings and where I think we are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this fairly explains the position at which we are. If one wants to determine the content of this motion, it will mean re-arguing everything that has been discussed before now and I really do not see the merit in doing that at this stage. I believe if there is any reason why any of the issues ought to be reopened in respect to a particular accused person, the Trial Chamber will consider doing that. I think you can invite the witness to continue the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Witness N (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Just remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Residovic. Take over the witness. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. N.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not hearing. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): To continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: He is not ... MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I would like to ask you, Mr. N, that we recall that at the end of the questioning we were discussing yesterday you said that in February 1996 for two days on 23rd and 24th February you made a lengthy statement to a representative of the prosecution. You also confirmed that you made a short statement, which you called differently, to a representative of the prosecution also, but in Belgrade. This second statement came after the request of the prosecution that you should make such a statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In making this statement during this brief integration, the interviewer was Mme Sabine Manke and the representative of the prosecution, Ms. Teresa McHenry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, during your first and second statements you signed those statements, saying that they contain all that, according to your knowledge and recollection, has been stated, that it was made on a voluntary basis, that it was truthful and that you are aware that it may be used in the proceedings before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, which is in great detail, and which contains facts about events and persons, you did not mention the name of Mr. Zejnil Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement -- I will read to you exactly what you said about Mr. Zejnil Delalic. You said: "Zejnil Delalic came several times. He was together with armed guards. He just looked around and I remember him talking to Delic. I personally saw Delalic in the hangar three times." Is that the statement that you made on 14th November 1996 in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you is that what you said. Will you answer with "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did not say three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the statement given to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You identified it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I read yesterday that I said that he came several times, not three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will Mr. N be given his statement that he identified yesterday? (Handed to witness). I will read it again: "Zejnil Delalic came on several occasions. He was together with armed guards. He just looked around, and I remember him addressing Delic. I personally saw Delalic in the hangar three times." That is the end of your statement; is that correct? Have I read the last sentence correctly: "I personally saw Delalic in the hangar three times"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Testifying before this Trial Chamber on pages 1925 and 1926 of the transcript you said that: "Zejnil Delalic came only once and that during that visit Hazim Delic fired a shot, which fired back at Davor Kuljanin who was treated medically." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I saw him in person. I didn't know him and that was when I saw him in person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the words: "I personally saw Delalic in the hangar three times", and "I personally saw Zejnil Delalic once" are quite contradictory statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you answer my question? Is "three times" and "once" a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it must have been an error in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is "three times" and "once" two opposite things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just now, Mr. N, you said that you do not know Mr. Zejnil Delalic, or, rather, that you did not know him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know him before. I learned from other people who knew him that it was Zejnil Delalic. Before that the guards would warn us that Zejnil Delalic was coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, even then when you saw him you had no personal knowledge of Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Other people told me that it was Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am repeating: in the statement of November 14th you said that he came three times. In your testimony before this Chamber you said once. Both times you said that you saw him personally. The first time, Mr. N, you said that each time you saw him, he just looked around in the hangar. Testifying before this Trial Chamber, you said that he came to Hangar Number 6 and that one -- a shot that was fired wounded a prisoner. These are details which it is difficult to forget, unless you are making them up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not making up anything. I am repeating there may be an error in the translation. I saw him when he came to the prison, but learning from others that he had come three times was what I said. I am sure that then I didn't say that I personally had seen him three times. I just said that he had come three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my questions? You had the opportunity to answer these questions already in the direct questioning, so I am now asking you about the differences between your evidence of 14th November and your testimony in court. Mr. N, let us go back to some other matters now, which you may be familiar with. Mr. N, you said that you were born and bred in the municipality of Konjic; is that correct? Before your arrest you said you had lived in the village of Viniste; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Konjic before the war there were members of at least three ethnic groups. The majority were Bosnian Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no interethnic conflicts among them before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war you did not see any conflicts among those people on ethnic grounds. They mixed, they worked together and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, you know that on April 6th the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a state of imminent war danger was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I wasn't involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you are a military conscript, Mr. N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that a general mobilisation had been called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not respond to the call for general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had Yugoslav citizenship, but I was living in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, I am asking you whether as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina you responded to the call for mobilisation; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive any call-up, and I was a citizen of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask to be relieved of your citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked that of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask to be excluded from citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can the court allow me to ask this question once again, if Mr. N can answer? Did you personally ask to be excluded from the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Will you answer by "yes" or "no", if you can? Did you ask to be excluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no need to be excluded, to ask for exclusion, when I was not a citizen. I was a citizen of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you never asked to be excluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but that is not the right question. I was not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I had Yugoslav citizenship written on all my documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist on this question. There is no need for my learned colleague to object. The regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina regulate the question of citizenship. It is not a question of personal choice, unless exclusion is requested. So you did not respond to the call for mobilisation to join the Territorial Defence or the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never called up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you knew that a certain number of people had responded to the call-up and joined the reserve police force and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask, Ms. Residovic, and the witness, to slow down in their question and answer, because we cannot follow well enough. Thank you very much. Excuse me for interrupting. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, Mr. Turone. Mr. N, are you familiar with the following persons: Milijan Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of him. I learned that they killed his father and that two of his brothers were killed, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Witness F, who testified before this court 20 days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Slobodan Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mitar Manivoda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mladen Zivak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which Zivak you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mladen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, you said that you knew many people in Konjic and in the surroundings of your village, and your village belongs to the local community of Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Milijan Cecez was a man living in that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these other persons, who you do not know in person, were also living in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not, because there were no Zivaks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Cecez, Slobodan Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. N, in January 1992 you applied to join the reserve force of JNA in the surroundings of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In January 1992 -- no, actually in February 1992 I was working for the JNA as a civilian until April 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, you were working in the JNA from January 18th until March 10th as a reserve soldier of the JNA, and you were on Mt Hum near Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period you received a salary from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was remunerated as a civilian working for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were then in the region of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that on Mt Hum heavy weapons were positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After March 10th, Mr. N, you went back to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Konjic on April 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not bring your rifle from Mostar; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were arrested, Mr. N, you said that your neighbour, a Muslim, a member of the TO, tried to protect you, together with some other local people; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were arrested by members of the HVO police, among whom there were both Muslims and Croats; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That evening they took us to that house, but before that we were taken to Konjic and then released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this HVO police, consisting of Muslims and Croats, had white belts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not HVO police. There were Croats and Muslims, and they were wearing white belts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then hand in any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't own any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, if a document or a witness says that you had weapons, you are claiming that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were arrested, we had no weapons. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if a document or a witness claims otherwise, then it is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, your father and brother were also in Celebici for a short time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father was not. My brother was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They are at home and they have no problems; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the Trial Chamber or these past few days, you said that you were interrogated by Mladen Zovko; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew Milijan Cecez; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So he left Donje Selo before you were arrested; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Lazar Cecez took over the duties from Milijan Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Let me repeat once again: in this hamlet of Viniste we were together with Croats. We had connections with our neighbours, our Muslims, and no other connections. We didn't meet or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, in answer to a question by Mr. Turone of the prosecution, you told this Trial Chamber about what you were asked by the interrogators in Celebici. However, you did not tell us what your answers were. Is it true that in that statement during the interrogation you said that you were given by Milijan Cecez an M-48 and 60 bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that, because that day when I was interrogated by Mladen Zovko, I had been beaten up before that. I just remember him asking me where I was from and whether I was armed when I was arrested. That's all I remember. I don't know what else they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- let me remind you -- that you said then that you were in the JNA reserve force for two months in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What I told you just now is what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you told them that you were working as a civilian for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I told them, that I had an eight-hour working day working as a civilian for the JNA and for that I had a salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, you stated here that you were beaten up in Celebici on the second day after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were in a very difficult condition; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was difficult for you to eat and before this Tribunal you said that other prisoners, that is Jordan Gotovac and the late Zjelko Klimenta, helped you to swallow some food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated in your first statement and also during your testimony that you were given milk, some liver, to drink and eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was liver paste. I couldn't swallow, so he gave me some with his finger.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, is this the regular food given to others as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not milk. A woman, Cedo Cecez's mother-in-law, managed to smuggle some milk in over the fence and this late prisoner gave it to me and the small liver paste had to be shared by three or four prisoners, and that is the liver paste they gave me. That was while we were in Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the milk came from the family of one of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was passed through the fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, you were in such a condition in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You pointed out that you found in that building Slobodan Babic, who was heavily injured. You also said that he had received those injuries during his arrest; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also noted that in that building Mirko Babic was there too, a cousin of Slobodan Babic. Mirko Babic is a man from the same village as Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Branko Gotovac was there too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that you were in the worst condition in the Building Number 22 with the exception of Slobodan Babic, of course, but I am talking about that period. Mr. N, can you agree with me that, in view of your condition while you were in Building 22, that if Mirko Babic, a relative and a neighbour, who was arrested together with Slobodan Babic and Branko Gotovac, in their testimony give certain details and facts related to the death of Slobodan Babic in a slightly different way from you, then what they say is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what they said. I said what I saw and what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated what you heard from others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your condition in Building 22 was worse than the condition of Mirko Babic and Branko Gotovac; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. N, in your first statement of February 1996 in connection with the death of Zjelko Klimenta, you said that it was the guard Padalovic who fired; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Padalovic said then that this was an accident; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Padalovic treated the prisoners correctly and with attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that after this event he was distressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that, because I didn't see him then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, when you said that he was very distressed, that he said that it was an accident, that he threw away his rifle and left and that you never saw him again, this is something that you did not say in your statement of February 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he was very distressed I didn't say; that we didn't see him again, that is true, and what else you said -- and what else that I said, that he treated us correctly, that is also true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If this is contained in your statement of February 1992, it means that the interrogators put in the statement, not respecting your will, something that you did not say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The words that you uttered I did not speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If they are contained in this statement, then you claim that somebody else put them down and that you did not utter them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be an error in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. N. Yesterday you recognised the photograph of a man with long hair and a pigtail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that you saw him in Hangar 6. Is it true that you saw him when he came to look for someone to wash his car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that. I know that he came in with a group of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That man was there also when Delic fired that shot? Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. I think this is the last of the questions from the defence. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no particular questions in re-examination. Simply we had an agreement with the defence lawyers about the photographs concerning the injuries of this witness, since the examination, medical examination report in the meantime arrived, but it has no photographs attachments. So defence lawyers inspected the injuries and agreed with us about the opportunity to have these photographs exhibited, tendered as an exhibit. So I would like to present these photographs as Exhibits 94, 95, etc. They are 11 photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to bring to the court's attention that not all defence attorneys inspected the wounds. I am the only one from the defence team that did personally inspect the wounds of Witness N. Because these photographs are being introduced at this time, I would only like for clarification purposes to be allowed to ask the witness one more question that has arisen from this examination relating to the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have two copies of this bunch of photos for the Chamber and for exhibition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. McMurrey is interested in asking further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have seen the photographs. I do not need to have them in front of me at this point. I just have one question for the witness for clarification. I believe that the photographs accurately represent the wounds that I viewed, but I believe it was on your right hand, Witness N -- we discussed several marks on your hand, but the most prominent being a puncture wound in the middle of your palm. I wanted it to be clear to the court that that puncture wound was a result of injury that you sustained after 1992 and after you were released from Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, there is a question relating to the transcript. The final question asked by my colleague was answered and the answer does not appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that today?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just now. The answer to the question was -- the question was -- the answer to the final question was "Yes". The question was: "That man was there also when Delic fired that shot?" and the answer was "Yes". The answer does not appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let her put the question again. It will now be part of the record. You can put the question. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this satisfies. You mean there was no translation of that? This is a multiplying effect of errors. Pose the question again so we can have a full translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. N, the person that you recognised in the photograph was present when Mr. Delic accidentally fired his rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise for these technical difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we will have a full translation of all the questions and answers. I think this is all you have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just to clarify an ambiguity, this person you recognised in picture number 3 shown to you yesterday is one of the persons you saw in Hangar 7 when Delic fired a bullet?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The question was just asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know if there is any Hangar 7 there. I do not remember any Hangar 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is that the person you previously talked about as Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is the person who was accompanying Zejnil Delalic and was joined by him in Hangar Number 6. That is the person whose photograph was shown to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: How did you get to know that one of those people was named Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. He has answered that question. He said it was told to him by someone else. There is no foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually he merely recognised the person as a person he has seen before in Hangar 6. He did not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. I have no more questions. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but the comment was that he had not -- that the witness had not known Zejnil Delalic before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is true. I think the witness can now be discharged. He is free.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now have a break and come at 11.45, in 30 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are ready to proceed with our next witness. We would call Mr. Golubovic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Invite him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His witness number? You must have numbered the witnesses. His witness number?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but unfortunately I do not have the number in front of me. 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness. MR. GOLUBOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue in direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, would you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): I am Miro Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask the usher's assistance in moving the ELMO down so I may see the witness? Sir, can you please tell us your age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born 19th September 1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. How far did you go in school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished the secondary school as an auto mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where are you from? Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In 1992 where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in Konjic in 15th September Street, number 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At this time in 1992 what kind of work were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working as a private taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In 1992 was there a time when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested in the month of May. I don't know the exact date, but in early May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At that time were you still living in Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that arrest I did not live in the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Prior to the arrest were you living in Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly what happened when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went from my apartment towards my family home in Donje Selo near the motel at the exit of Konjic I was stopped by the police and I was detained in the motel. They searched my car and Amir Begic said that I could go home. However, the Commander of the police station in Konjic, Sevko Niksic, said I had an apartment in Konjic and we needed to go to have a search of the apartment done. We went to my apartment and they searched it, and they took me to the police station in Konjic. I waited there until 1 o'clock at night, and because of my father's and some friends' intervention Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, who was the principal of the municipality, allowed me to go to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did you go after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to my family home in Donje Selo, in the hamlet of Cerici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when in May this was when you were arrested and then released later that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was before May 6th, but I don't know the exact date. It was before 6th May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a time when there was any kind of fighting or military action in your village or hamlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a military action on May 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Prior to the attack were you armed, prior to the military action -- I am sorry -- were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was armed several days before the armed action.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you involved in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take part in the defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Prior to the actual military action had you been involved in any sort of patrols or preparation for possible military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came from the town to the village my mother criticised me for not taking part in these village watches, because she was ashamed that I would let other people defend or protect our home. So several days before the military action I took part in these watches.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a machine gun, 762, with a fold-up butt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened to you during and after the military action in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the military action started, the shells started falling in the village and people took shelter in the creeks and surrounding caves, and I was among them. Then they got in touch with the commanders of the TO and they negotiated a surrender and turning over of the weapons, and at that time I didn't have the courage to surrender myself, and I stayed for ten or fifteen days in the village until my mother got in touch with the members of the HVO military police and I surrendered to them, together with my weapons, and they took me to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just explain a little bit more what you mean when you say your mother got in touch with the HVO military police and you surrendered? Can you just explain that a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. No problem: there was a person in the military police who went to school with my sister, and when he saw that I wasn't among the prisoners who were brought to Celebici, he came to my mother to ask her if she knew where I was and whether she had any contact with me, and that it would be better for me to surrender than to continue on in the woods, because he said that there would only be some verification process in Celebici, and since I was not involved in anything I should be afraid about, then I decided to surrender, and they gave me a certificate that I would not be mistreated if I surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just explain who you surrendered to and what you remember about this certificate, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I surrendered to Darko Verkic, Mario Maric, Miro Vranic -- Miro or Ante; I don't know the first name exactly -- and then Jozic, whose nickname was Aga, and then there were several other guys there whose names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened after you surrendered? Who brought you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These same persons took me to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was the date that you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Celebici on June 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long in all did you stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Celebici from 6th June until 17th July.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Celebici did you learn who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not learn that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened -- please now tell us exactly what happened when you were brought to Celebici by these persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Celebici camp Milovan Kuljanin and I were waiting in the van until they came out and took us to the back part of the camp, where the manhole was and that's where they brought us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Milovan Kuljanin, who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a man who gave himself in together with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who brought you to the back part of the camp? Was that the same persons who brought you to Celebici itself or different people?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. She is leading the witness. He never said this manhole was in the back part of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just look at the transcript, the witness said: "They took us to the back part of the camp, to the manhole."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was it the same people who brought you to the back part of the camp -- was it the same people who brought you to the camp or different people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were present, but we were taken there by a driver called Berislav Stanic, and Mr. Hazim Delic was there present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened when you were brought to the back part of the camp? Please just tell us exactly what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They locked us up in the manhole and the HVO policeman intervened, and they opposed this, and they said that in the certificate it was said that we should be locked up in a special place, and that this was that special place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to explain this to us again. When you say "they", just explain who you mean. When you say they locked you up in the manhole and they said it was in the certificate, can you just explain that, so we understand exactly who "they" is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the guards who were in the camp, Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them who either put you in the manhole or who were present when you were placed in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We entered it ourselves, but Hazim Delic was present and Bero Stanic. I knew the two of them and I didn't know the others, and the HVO policemen were there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it, if you know, who said that it was in the certificate that you should be put in a special place and the manhole was this special place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Verkic said this, because he went to investigate to see why we had been put there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Did this conversation occur at the time while you were there being put into the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while we were entering the manhole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to ask, sir, that you look in front of you at Prosecution Exhibit 2. I am referring to this large model. I ask if you recognise what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a model of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask, if you can -- the logistics of this are not very easy -- if you could stand up and then just leaning over the table, so that the microphone can still pick up your voice, can you explain to the judges exactly what parts of the camp that you recognise and just in detail everything that you recognise about the camp. If you can, if you can recognise the front gate, would you please start with the front gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the front gate over there. (Pointing). This is the quarters, the store house, the hospital, the scales. This was Tunnel Number 9 with other supporting facilities like the manholes. This part of the camp over here I am not very familiar with. I only know the manhole I was in here in the corner, but I never entered the other building, Number 6 and the others, I never went to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please show us where the manhole you were brought and put into is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The manhole I stayed in at first is this one. (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down now. Let me also ask with the assistance of the technical unit for the witness to be shown on the computer Prosecution Exhibit 1, page 29, photo 38. Sir, I ask that you look at the screen in front of you and tell me if you recognise what that is? Sir, is there a picture in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you recognise what it is? I am sorry, sir. Do you recognise what is in the picture in front of you and, if so, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't hear anything. Oh, it's all right now. It's all right now. I didn't hear the question. I am sorry. Something must have been wrong with the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I am asking if you can recognise what is in the picture in front of you and, if so, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the manhole I was locked up in on the first day I arrived at the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the manhole two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anyone else put in the manhole at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me was Milovan Kuljanin and later a man was brought in whom I didn't know then, but I learned later that his name was Vlado Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what the conditions were like in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the manhole we didn't have enough air. We were afraid. The guards would come and beat on the lid. They would insult us and utter provocations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: After you were put in the manhole was the lid open or closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered it, it was open, but when we got inside it was closed and locked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened after two to three hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know how long it was, but I think it was Mr. Hazim Delic, he called me out to come out of the manhole, and when I came out, I saw Mr. Zdravko Mucic, who was sitting on a wooden bed, and I approached him. He asked me: "Where have you been, Golub?", and I asked him, if he could, to release me from that manhole, because we didn't have enough air. He said that he could not do that for me straightaway, that he had to ask some people who were interrogating the prisoners to take a statement from me, and then most probably they would transfer me to another part of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you said you were called Golub, can you tell us what does Golub mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does it mean anything? Maybe the interpreters can help. Does it mean anything, Golub? Is it anything besides a nickname? Sir, do you know if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in my life it doesn't mean anything else but my nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. If somebody -- well, that is fine. Did you know Mr. Mucic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I knew him by sight. We weren't friends, but we knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened next, after your conversation with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I went back to the manhole and Mr. Hazim Delic gave me a bottle of water, and after some time, maybe half an hour, Berislav Stanic came for me and he took me to the headquarters to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Again I am going to ask if you could just stand up and show, using the model, if you can, and if you have to move away from the model, you can, first where the conversation with Mr. Mucic took place and then where you were brought afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, (pointing), and then they took me this way. They drove me to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just let the record reflect that the first place the witness pointed to is known as J on the map. My eyes are not good enough to see the other one. I believe there is evidence about where the command centre was. What happened then, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reached the command building, they took me to an office and there I found Mladen Zovko, known as Kuhar, and another elderly man, whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They, after -- since I had grown up with Mladen Zovko, he said: "Where have you been? Nobody knows anything about you." Then he asked what I had by way of armaments and where I had been all that time, and I explained. I said where I was after the village was captured. I explained this to him. I can't remember exactly whether I signed that statement or not. Anyway, he said he'd finished and I was transferred by the guards to the part of the camp known as the prison hospital. I didn't know that at the time, but when I entered, I saw people lying on beds and some doctors, and they explained to me that it was the prison hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back for one minute to clarify a few matters. Was your relationship with -- can you describe what your relationship with Mr. Mucic was like prior to the time you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you ask about our relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You may have said this before, and I am sorry. I do not remember. Were you friends with Mr. Mucic beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't -- we were not friends or enemies. He was close to a relative of mine and they kept company, so we knew each other through this association between Mr. Mucic and my relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How do you feel about Mr. Mucic now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have friendly feelings for Mr. Mucic, as before the war, for instance, we were not very close. I didn't have any special feelings for him, nor did he for me, but after everything that he did for me, I have friendly feelings for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I am going to ask the usher's assistance -- maybe, in fact, if I could just use my case manager to take the top off what I believe is referred to as building B. Sir, I am going to direct your attention to the large model to your left. Tell me if you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I didn't hear any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just tell me if you recognise what building B -- I am sorry -- what the model is with number B on it that is in front of you to your left that does not have a top on it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a model of the command building of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you show me -- can you, using that model, show us where it was that you were interviewed by Kuhar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interviewed in this first room, left from the entrance (pointing).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would the windows of that room face the interior of the camp or the exterior of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They face in the direction of the prison hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Thank you. Please go on with what happened to you after your interrogation, where you were brought and what happened to you then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the prison hospital and I was there until 1.00 am. I sat by the door and one of the guards called my name. I can't remember now who he was and he took me out, and then I saw a police car in front of the administrative building, and in the office in which Zovko had interrogated me Sevko Niksic was sitting, the Commander of the police station, and Jasmin Guska, Secretary of the Minister of the Interior in Konjic. I don't know exactly his post but he had a higher rank than Sevko Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to a room at the end of the corridor on the left and these people who were taking me there were Jasmin Guska and a JNA man called Miralem Duracic, and a young man, younger than me, a blond man, whom I didn't know, and Mr. Hazim Delic would come in occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they entered, they switched off the light. There was very little light. I don't know where it was coming from, whether it was from the outside or maybe there was a light bulb inside. I couldn't see that. They brought a candle, which they lit on the table. Mr. Guska Jasmin questioned me about certain things and asked me certain questions, which I couldn't answer. He said he had finished and he asked Narcis, whom he addressed as Captain: "Captain, take things over." He lit the candle. He had scissors in his hands, which he heated in the flames and he burnt me in the area of the neck with the red hot scissors, and on the upper lip. A number of times with these heated scissors he would point them at me so that I should hold them, saying: "Cool them off a little." Also present was Miralem Duracic, known as Dura. Later they told me to raise my hands and they beat me in the area of the ribs, Hazim Delic on one side and this boy on the other. The boy I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Hazim Delic took me to the bathroom to wash and he told me to hurry up. He says: "Hurry up. They'll kill you.". Then he took me to a room -- I didn't know that it was a part of the camp known as Number 9. He opened the door and I went in. By the smell you could smell urine, and I saw that there were people inside, and when it dawned, I saw that they were some people from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you stay in this -- can you describe what this room Number 9 was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a tunnel. I don't know exactly how long it was, but there were about 30 or 40 people in there. It was narrow. It was narrow. Anyway I couldn't lie down normally there. I couldn't stretch out widthwise. At the bottom of the tunnel there was a bucket for our toilet needs, and there was some liquid on the floor. It had a stink and there were even some worms there. Whether it was water or urine I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long altogether did you stay in Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Tunnel 9 I stayed I think about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What were the food and water facilities in the tunnel? How did you eat and get water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The water was okay. It was clean. It wasn't dirty. We were given it in an aluminium can, a military can that used to be used for food. The quantity wasn't sufficient, but it was clean. Food, we would get a piece of bread a day and during the time I was there in Number 9 maybe a couple of times we were given some cooked food, three spoonfuls each.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. While you were in the tunnel were you ever subjected to any additional mistreatment other than what you have already testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After spending two days in the tunnel I was mistreated. One evening they took me out -- the guards took me out of Number 9 and they took me above Number 9 maybe some 20 metres away to a plateau, and there there were quite a large number of soldiers. In front of me they took Zaro Mrkajic and after me I learned later, when I returned to Number 9, they took Damir Djordjic, who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when I got there Bato Alkadic was beating Zaro Mrkajic and I was sitting on some kind of concrete plateau. I was sitting there and watching them beating Zaro. Then I noticed and recognised some people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised some people among those soldiers and police then: Jasmin Guska, Sevko Niksic, Dzumhur Sadik known as "Diksa". Then there was Pero, "Srbija", Blazevic his surname. I need to mention him because I recognised his voice, and when Alkadic was beating me, he was saying: "It's enough. You'll kill him." There were some other people there that I did not recognise. There was an older man with grey hair. He hit me a couple of times, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they finished with Zaro Mrkajic, they took him away, and then Bato Alkadic approached me and asked me whether I knew him. I said I did and he asked me about some good things that we had shared, whether I had done him any service and he me, and I said I knew about all that, that we were friends, but he said: "But we are no longer friends and you are no longer my friend, nor is Keljo." This is a man who was killed in the camp. His name was Zjelko Klimenta. He ordered me to kneel and he started hitting me with his feet. He fired next to my head and at one point he hit me with his pistol on the forehead and with his knife just below the eye and he made a cut in my skin. I don't know exactly how long this went on, but while he was doing all these things I noticed that some other people would manage to hit me a couple of times, so that he wasn't quite alone. He wasn't doing the job all alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue with what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before he started beating me, that is Bato Alkadic, Mr. Hazim Delic came with a flashlight, opened a lid and asked -- he showed this to Sevko Niksic. He lifted the lid a little and Sevko nodded. And said yes. Later I realised he was pointing to the manhole where I was put in afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue with what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they put me into this manhole, in fact, I lowered myself -- as I rolled over, I held on to a rail with my hands. It was maybe four or five metres deep and I went all the way down. There was some water there which had the smell of urine. I washed myself a little bit. Several hours passed. I heard some steps approaching. They opened the lid and the voice said: "Golub, are you alive?" I don't know the person's first name but his name was Macic, and he asked me whether I could climb up, so he could give me some water. I asked him to take me back to Number 9, because my pelvis was injured and I wanted to get some help from other people. I was afraid that I would lose consciousness and then I would drown in that water underneath. Then he said: "No, you can't do it right now. They are still there. I can't let you go now. I can't take you back but as soon as they leave", he said, "I'll take you back to Number 9." So that's what happened. Maybe a number of hours passed and he took me back to Number 9 and left me there with the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please, using again the model, show us where Tunnel 9 is, show us where you were beaten and, if you can, show us where the manhole that you have just talked about is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing). Tunnel Number 9 is here and I was beaten here and I don't know which of these three manholes it was that they put me in. I can't say exactly which manhole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That was the manhole you first talked about at the end of this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is another manhole he is now talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This is another manhole, that is correct. Sir, am I correct that this is a different manhole than the one you were put in when you were first brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In this picture I only have one manhole, in these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Just for your information, your Honour, if you also want to look at page 37, photograph 50, I believe that is a photograph of the area that the witness has just ... During the time that you stayed in Number 9, Tunnel Number 9, sir, was this the only time that you yourself were mistreated, what you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only time. The first time was in the administrative building and that was the second time, and after that nobody mistreated me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were any other prisoners, to your knowledge, subjected to mistreatment, any prisoners from Tunnel 9 subjected to mistreatment during the time you spent in Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were acts of provocation and of people mistreated. There was Rajko Djordjic. He was being taken to be beaten a number of times, and there was Desimir and Zjelko Milosovic. He was taken from Number 9 and was probably killed. I have never saw him come back and he was not among the living ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you yourself saw or heard with respect to how Zeljko Milosovic was treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Milosovic was frequently taken out and he would come back all wet. We would give him something to put on. He was there for several days, three or four days while I was there, and was taken three or four times and finally didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, what kind of -- what was your physical condition during the time that you were in Tunnel Number 9, both after the first beating and then after the second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in a poor shape. I could not get up. People had to help me to get up. I couldn't move much, and I was exhausted, because there was not enough food and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did anyone other than the other prisoners ask you about how you received your injuries or offer you any sort of assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We helped each other as much as we could. They knew -- Zarko Mrkajic asked me when I came back to Number 9 -- he asked me whether I knew who beat us. I told him I didn't know and he said he knew and he was going to tell me, but I knew who beat me. I didn't dare tell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides the other prisoners, did anyone besides the prisoners ever ask you about your injuries or offer you any sort of assistance in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Mucic asked me on one occasion when I was taken out by the guards. He asked me whether I knew who beat me. I was afraid to tell him, and I said that I didn't know. Then he said that he would learn and to tell me who it was who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just please explain to us in more detail exactly what happened on this occasion that you referred to, if you know approximately when it was you were in the tunnel, exactly when the conversation took place, if you could just please tell us this in detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day or two after my last beating Zdravko Mucic came and asked me these things, who beat me and everything I just said, and among other things, he asked me, since my father had some hunting rifles and those weapons were not turned in, and people from the MUP had that as a basis for beating me, so Zdravko Mucic asked me whether I knew where these rifles were, so they could be turned in, so that this mistreatment would stop. Then my father came, who said that he knew, because he was detained in Number 6; he came over and he said that he knew where those were, and that he was going to take them so that they could get it. So my father was then taken back home and he probably turned those in to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just go back. First of all, where did this conversation take place? Was it inside the tunnel or outside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
