utterances.text: The conversation, it was outside the tunnel, across the road, across the entrance -- across the gate to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How was it that you came to be at that place? Did someone ask you? Did you go yourself? Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called out and then I was helped to get out by Branislav Mrkajic and Branislav Kuljanin. They helped me to get out. It was several metres, maybe 3, 4, 5 metres from the entrance to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When they helped you get out, can you just describe: was Mr. Mucic standing? Were you standing? Can you just please explain the positions of the people and who else was present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was sitting on a fence. There was a metal fence, and Hazim Delic was standing next to him, and I was sitting on the pavement, on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that your father just -- how was it that your father came to be there also? Did he just -- was he walking by? Did someone get him? Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't by accident he was passing. Mr. Mucic asked me what was the reason, why were they beating me, "What are they looking for?", and I told him the main reason for my being beaten was these weapons, these hunting weapons that my father possessed. He said did I know about this, so we would resolve this. I said I didn't know. He said: "Does Slavko know?", because that was my father, and I said he probably did because they were his. Then my father was brought there to tell where this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic say anything to your father? Did you hear that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point I heard him say -- he said: "What is more important, these rifles or people's lives?" My father started crying and he said he knew where this was. It was buried a few months ago and that he was going to give it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it who said to your father: "What's more important, these rifles or people's lives?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He has already answered that question. He has said: "I heard him say ...", in answer to the question: "Did Mr. Mucic say anything to your father?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Counsel is correct. I am sorry. I did not realise it was clear on the transcript. Thank you. What happened after that, after the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this conversation I was taken back to Number 9 and my father -- and this is what I learned later, when I came -- when I was released from the camp -- my father went home and turned in those weapons. In fact, Mr. Mucic, when my father turned in these weapons, he went to Number 9. He said that the weapons had been turned in, that there are no problems now, that I shouldn't worry, that they will have nothing to look for any more, and then at that time he also brought a blanket and a shaving kit from my home and Emir Dzajic, the guard, brought that to me to Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have any other conversations with Mr. Mucic about your physical condition after the one that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was several days after what I just mentioned. He came over and asked -- I was moving slowly. He said: "What's up, Golub?" I told him I was in poor shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I had dizzy spells and things like that, and he said that he would see if he could help me somehow so that I could be transferred to the prison hospital. He said: "Most probably you will be less mistreated there and you will be more protected there because that is close to the administrative building and there's always people there", so they won't have an opportunity to beat me and I wouldn't -- nobody would know who did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe several -- maybe a day passed, maybe half a day passed since this conversation, and I was taken to the prison hospital, Number 22, and I was there until I was released from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who brought you to Number 22, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were two or three guards and among them was this Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Landzo before you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Landzo. We lived in the same street in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo ever mistreat you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Landzo in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him a couple of times. He came to the door. Once he brought in a dog to the door. He did not enter ever. I never saw him entering Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened on the occasion he brought the dog to the tunnel, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He brought him to the door and he was saying something to us, but I don't recall what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now when you said you were brought to Building Number 22, is that the medical station that you have already referred to in your testimony? Are those the same place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the same place, the hospital and that Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Building Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until 17th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever perform any work while you were in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was let out to clean, to pick up the cigarette stubs and I was cleaning out the kitchen and restaurant area, but never any heavy physical work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, why were you chosen to do these chores?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was probably one of the healthier people in the hospital, so maybe that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just generally describe what conditions were like when you were in 22, including the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Building Number 22 the conditions were much better than in Number 9. We had beds to lie on except for one mattress, which was on the floor. We had food. Maybe there were moments or maybe a couple of days when there was no food, but the conditions were generally much more tolerable than in Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know where the food for the prisoners came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was coming from the town. They were bringing it in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know where the foods from the -- for the guards came from? Did they eat the same food that the prisoners ate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they did not eat the same food, but I don't know where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever get any food besides the food that you received as a prisoner, the same food that other prisoners received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I had an opportunity when I was cleaning the restaurant to eat some food, the left-over food that was on the plates. On one occasion Mr. Hazim Delic gave me some bacon to eat, and before my release from the prison Mr. Pavo Mucic shared from the same plate that he was eating from, he shared some roast meat with me, skewered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you spent in the medical station, Number 22, did you ever see Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic came to the hospital several times while I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to speak with him during those times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not talk to him. Sometimes he would smile at me or wink at me, but mostly we did not talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversations with him when you were outside doing any chores, doing your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never talked to him about anything. On one occasion he came -- he had come back from fishing and he gave me two packs of cigarettes. He said that I was smoking too much and that I shouldn't do that for health reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were out doing your chores, were you allowed free access to all parts of the camp, allowed to walk around wherever you wanted, or was it limited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not allowed to walk around. We would work where we were told to go to work, so this is where we would be moving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go near the fence, to the outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I never left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever given any instructions about whether you should or should not approach the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion Mr. Mucic said that even if I was told to do something, that it would be desirable not to come close to the fence, because some of the guards could kill me and could claim that I had tried to escape. So they could stage that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct, sir, that you yourself did not suffer any mistreatment while you stayed in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Building 22 nobody ever mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to enter a new area that will probably take five or ten minutes to discuss. I do not know if you would like me to start that or have the lunch break now. I am happy to do either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is preferable you have the lunch break, so we return fresh later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to inform you that Mr. Turone this afternoon is proofing a witness, so he cannot be present in the court room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Inform him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during the time that you were in the medical station did you ever observe any prisoners being mistreated either inside the medical station or at some location outside the medical station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital I didn't see anyone mistreated, but I did see it outside, within the camp, what I could see from the medical station. In the part of the camp that could be seen from the medical station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please tell us, if you can, any specific incidents of mistreatment that you observed while you were in the medical station of things happening outside the medical station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I saw through the window in front of Tunnel Number 9 when Mr. Delic Hazim beat a prisoner, whose name I learned afterwards was Susic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just please tell us exactly what you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him beating him with either water or electricity cable. Then he left it. Then he broke off a piece of wood and he beat him with that piece of wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there anyone else besides Mr. Delic present during this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time also present was Mr. Esad Landzo, and later, when Susic sat on the asphalt, he dragged him by the arms. I don't know exactly what he was doing to him, but something with his hands. It was quite far away, so I couldn't see exactly what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the assistance of the technical people, I would like to show the witness a portion of Prosecution Exhibit 3, which is the video taken of the camp. There is already just a 30-second excerpt that I would like to show the witness, with the assistance of the video unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I just ask you to look at the screen in front of you and watch it and tell me if you recognise anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only see the court room at present, nothing else. I see now the medical station, the entrance to the prison hospital, and I see the window inside through which I could see what I just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. As you look at the film, if you remember, can you tell us which of the windows it was or what area approximately it was that you saw this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this from the right-hand side window when you enter the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe the kind of window it was and how you were able to see out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The window could be opened only about one quarter of the way, probably for the purpose of ventilation, and then one could see the part of the compound in front of Number 9?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the assistance. That is fine. Sir, if you could just stand up and, using that pointer, could you just show using the model where it was approximately that Mr. Susic -- the person that you later learned was Mr. Susic was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That must have been somewhere here, a little below the doors of Number 9, here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down. During the time that you were in the medical station approximately how many persons were -- prisoners were also kept in the medical station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember some names, but about 10-12 people were in there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was -- I am sorry. Could you just explain: when you say there were about 10-12 people in there all the time, do you mean the same 10-12 people were always there, or do you mean that people came and went, with there generally being around 10 or 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people who would come for bandaging. Then there were people for medical treatment, but there were about 10 there regularly. There were so many places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were persons who stayed there ever released from the infirmary, ever recovered enough such that they left the infirmary while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there no one was released from the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say "released", do you mean released from the camp or released from the infirmary to go to another part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that you were asking whether they were released home from the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know -- and I understand your answer to that to be "no" -- do you know whether or not persons were ever taken out of the infirmary and placed in other parts of the camp without being released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases of people being discharged from the infirmary and transferred to another part of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember who any of those persons were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Milovan Kuljanin and Zjelko Klimenta, when they were transferred to Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you remember about their transfer? Do you know who ordered it, who told them they were being transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who ordered it and who said, but I just know that Mr. Hazim Delic came for them and told them to get ready, to pick up their things and to go back to Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: While you were in the medical station, was it ever visited by any journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were journalists. I think that they were from some Arab countries. I am not sure. I don't know exactly, but there were some people of dark skin, and they spoke a language unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just describe exactly what you remember about their visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember they came inside and they asked me whether I had participated in the fighting against the Muslims, whether I had fired. I said no, and I said that I couldn't shoot at my neighbours, and he was not satisfied with my answer, and he stood on my stomach while he questioned another prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many journalists there were or people with the journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the building there were quite a number of people. I think that Mr. Mucic was there too and inside there were two journalists and a photographer and a translator.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you hear any conversation between Mr. Mucic and any of the journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion then I heard -- I don't know who he was talking to -- but he said that he couldn't force anyone to say something that he had not done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As far as you could tell during your entire time -- the court's indulgence for one second, please. Sir, during the entire time you were at the camp both in Tunnel Number 9 and in Building 22 were there times when you noticed the treatment either to you or to other prisoners was better or worse than other times, and, if so, could you correlate that with anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never noticed that the treatment was improving while I was there. It was always the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when was it that you were released -- I am sorry. I believe you have already testified that you were released on July 17th. Can you please tell us exactly what happened on the day you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day I was released from the camp it was the morning. They brought to the infirmary Bosko Samoukovic, who had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who brought him to the infirmary, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought in by some prisoners and they were accompanied by Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the man was moaning and Esad Landzo said that he had to recover in half an hour. He told the doctors to get him well in half an hour. However, he died five minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt for one minute while you are telling about the day you were released. Do you remember when, approximately, the first time you saw Mr. Landzo in Celebici camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Landzo in Celebici camp that evening when they took me for interrogation. I was taken by Sevko Niksic and Guska. He was standing at the entrance of the administrative building of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please go on, sir, and tell us what happened the day you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosko died and we put him down on the mattress that was in the corner next to the door of the Building 22. At that moment a lady, Jasna Dzuhmur, walked in to take some paper. We had covered Bosko with a sheet. She never even asked who it was or what it was, as if it was a dead dog lying there. When Landzo peeped in I was sitting on the bed. He said: "Why don't you lie down?", thinking that I was afraid to lie on the same bed on which a man had died five minutes earlier. At that minute one of the guards called me out and took me to the prison dining room, where I saw Mr. Mucic, Bato Alikadic and Pero Blazevic, known as "Srbija".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUCIC THEN SAID
utterances.text: "Look, Golub hasn't eaten for three days". I smiled a little, because I had eaten. The previous day I had had some cabbage in the kitchen while I was cleaning up, and he was eating some meat and he offered me to eat from his plate, and as I was hungry, I started to eat normally. Then he said -- he asked the people to grill some more meat for us, to fry some more meat for us. Then the cook said she didn't have any more oil. Then he told me to follow him. When I got to the van I opened the door and saw my father inside, and my relative, Milorad Golubovic, who was sitting in the van, and I asked them: "Where are we going?" They said they didn't know, so I asked Pavo. I asked him whether I should take my things with me and he said that I should. So I assumed I was being taken somewhere and that I would not be returning to Celebici, since he told me to take my things. So when we left from the camp, we were in the back part of the van. Mr. Zdravko Mucic and a driver from the camp were sitting in front. He was driving. We could see through the wind-shield where we were going. On the way we stopped and picked up some women, who were carrying food to the camp for their relatives, who were in prison there. I saw that we were turning in the direction of my house, and when we stopped, I got out. My mother ran up to me and we sat in front of the house, and then Mr. Mucic took out paper, or rather the discharge paper from the camp, and he said to me: "Here you are. Now you can stay home. I know how good that is. That is not so good and I am not sure I have helped you very much, because here you can get killed by anyone."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At that time were you told anything by Mr. Mucic or anyone else at that time about why you had been chosen to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't say anything why I had been chosen to be released. I was released, my father, and my relative, Milorad Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Afterwards were you ever told by Mr. Mucic or anyone else why you had been released, at any later point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody said why I was released. I always wondered why I was imprisoned. I never thought why I was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you: the release -- the discharge paper you received, can you briefly describe it? I would ask the usher's assistance, please. I am handing the usher the original and a translation for exhibition. Here are three copies for the judges. Defence counsel has already received these. I would ask that it be marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are these release papers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe this is Prosecution Exhibit 95. If you would just show the witness the original. The translation is not of assistance, I believe. Sir, I am showing you what has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 95 for identification purposes. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this release paper that I received from Mr. Zdravko Mucic upon leaving the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Can I ask the usher again now to put this on the ELMO. I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not disputed, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Well -- I was just going to ask him a couple of questions about it, but if your Honours would prefer to look at their copies. Sir, I am going to ask you: do you recognise whose signature is on -- is that your discharge document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my discharge document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whose signature appears on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How can he know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I can ask him if he knows. If he knows, he can state it; if he does not, he can state it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is he familiar with the signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whose signature is on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here in a biro "Zejnil Delalic". I don't know whether that is his signature, but I know what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct, sir, that you were not present when this document was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did your father also receive a discharge document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father received a similar discharge document, but he doesn't have it on him now. He lost it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see your father's discharge document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was identical to mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you know that because you saw it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw it, only this limitation on movement was different. In my father's case it applied to the village of Cerici and in my case to the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were granted permission to go anywhere you wanted within the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could move around, though I didn't. Mr. Mucic was explaining to me: "It's a good thing that's what it says." If somebody comes to look for me, then my family can say I have gone somewhere else within the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever told why there was a difference between your -- where you were permitted to go and where your father was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Simply for the sake of my own security; that was the explanation I was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, at this time I would like to move into evidence Prosecution Exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. After you were released, sir, did you ever have occasion to see Mr. Mucic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him four or five times. He would come to my home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally why he would come to see you or just briefly what would the -- what you know about the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came several times bringing cigarettes. He brought medicine for my mother, because my mother is a serious diabetes patient. He would come by to see what I was doing. We would talk. I asked him to help me to go to cross over to Serb-held territory, but he kept persuading me to stay on, not to go, that the worst was behind us, and then one day when he came, when I made the same proposal, he said: "It might not be a bad idea", that the situation had changed, and that I should go; I should abandon my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately when was this conversation, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was about the beginning of November, because I left some ten days after that on 10th November, so it was at the very beginning of November or the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, who assisted in your release? I am sorry. Who assisted in your leaving Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was about to leave Konjic Mr. Zdravko Mucic came and asked me whether I had confidence in a man who was supposed to take me, and he was Zjelko Mlikota. I said that yes, I did have confidence in him and I had nothing against him driving me to Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that Mr. Mlikota did drive you to Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mlikota drove me to Ilidza, the Terma Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During any of your conversations with Mr. Mucic after you were released was Mr. Zejnil Delalic ever mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion Mr. Mucic mentioned Mr. Zejnil Delalic, when I came to collect some Red Cross relief that was being distributed in the house of Mr. Zoran Cecez. Mr. Mucic told me that the flour that we had received could not have been provided by him, had it not been for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, who had had certain problems on account of these -- of giving this flour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Zejnil Delalic in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay I never saw Mr. Zejnil Delalic in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of Mr. Zejnil Delalic's brothers in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw in the camp when the journalists came that I was talking about a moment ago; I saw Zejnil Delalic's brother, Dzemal, and I saw one of his nephews, who was living in Prizor, who came to the infirmary. I don't remember his name but I know he belongs to Mr. Zejnil Delalic's family.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I am going to go back for a minute to the first part of your testimony, when you were in the first manhole at the end of the camp. When you were taken out of the manhole, what happened to Mr. Milovan Kuljanin? Was he also taken out or did he remain in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He stayed on in the manhole after me. I don't know what happened to him. I saw him for the first time after that when I was in the infirmary, and he was in the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Again going back here, you have described several times when you were asked questions by Mr. Kuhar and then by some other members of the MUP. Was there ever any other time when you were asked questions in a formal kind of way and in a formal interrogation or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any formal interrogations except when I was questioned by Jasmin Guska without any record having been kept, without any documents or papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You have mentioned before, sir, that one of the people who brought you to the camp was Mr. Darko Verkic; did you ever see him in the camp other than when he first brought you to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you please describe the circumstances under which you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Verkic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Verkic came to the Celebici camp after he left me. Two or three days later he took me out. That was when I was burnt on the neck. He took me outside the warehouse building in the camp and he asked me who had done that to me, and I didn't dare tell him, and he was surprised. Afterwards he said that he was trying to help me, but I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion with him about the interrogation that had gone on and who was in charge or who was responsible or involved with the administration of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to him about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So is it correct that you never discussed with Mr. Verkic anything about the questioning of prisoners and how that was being handled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't remember, but we didn't talk about that. He asked me who had beaten me, and he said something to the effect that he could not help me, that he wasn't there, but nothing very specific about any of those things that you are asking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct there was also no discussion with Mr. Verkic about the relationship between the HVO and the TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend has taken the horse to water twice and he has not drunk. I think that is enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I am allowed in the circumstances to ask the witness to be sure if he remembers something. Then I think to the extent that I have guided him a little more than usual, it would go to the weight rather than to the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you ask if you can lead him into it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I am entitled to clarify whether or not, in fact, his recollection is exhausted. I do not believe this is such an extreme example of leading questions, and I believe if he answers -- I do not know what his answer will be -- it would go to the weight rather than to the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, if a witness cannot remember something, he cannot be cross-examined, because that is what it is, cross-examined as to his recollection by the party who has called him. It is cross-examination, not leading. That is not permissible, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What actually do you want the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I want to be clear whether or not this witness remembers having any conversation with Mr. Verkic about the relationship between the TO and HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And he does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in general he says he does not remember much about the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is the answer. If he does not remember, that is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would ask to be allowed to double-check that, but if your Honours forbid it, it is your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has given you his answer. What do you want him to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I gather the objection is sustained and I may not ask that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is because it was answered. The question was answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you know whether or not there were any women in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were women in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you yourself ever see the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw these women personally at the gate when we came out to have a drink of water and in those moments I would see some of these women.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, who were the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not know, but now I know they were some of my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. The court's indulgence. Sir, just finally, since the time you left Konjic, have you had any communication with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no communications with Mr. Mucic except for one occasion when I received a greeting card from Mr. Mucic. I don't know if it was Christmas. In the meantime a son was born to me and he congratulated me on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When approximately was this? Around what Christmas time? I mean, what year is what I am trying to get.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was -- I think it was this last Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you decided the order for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will proceed in this order. First, counsel for Mr. Delic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Landzo; and, fourth, counsel for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I am going to ask you some questions, and. Just so there is no surprises, I will tell you basically the order I am going to do things in. First I am going to ask you some things about your village and the defence of your village; then I want to talk a little bit about the camp and some of the things that happened there; then I want to go through my notes about what you testified to. It may be kind of random. If you do not understand one of my questions, will you stop me, and I will rephrase the question so you understand it? Will you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Yes, I did understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not getting any translation, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You will do that for me. If you will listen to my question and just answer the question that I asked, we will all be out of here quicker. Fair enough? The first thing I want to talk to you about is the weapon you had. It was a 7.62 mm machine gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got that from my neighbour, Dragan Sinikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know where he got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He may even have bought it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Were there a lot of weapons like that machine gun around your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent a short period of time in my village. I had this one machine gun and it would have been better had I not had that one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, but did a lot of other people have weapons like that around your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village I know that Novica Draganic, who is a relative of mine on my mother's side, he had a machine gun like that. He turned it in and I don't know of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Novica Draganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He had a machine gun also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: About how many people were there besides him that were in this group you had that was patrolling the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Novica Draganic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said on your direct examination -- I can find my notes on it -- basically, as I recall, what you said was there was a group of people that patrolled your village and your mother talked to you about not being in that. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I remember, yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: About how many folks were in that group? How many people were in that group that were patrolling the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four persons who would sort of walk through the village, then maybe drink half a litre of brandy and then went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can understand. Okay. So it was a rather informal group, as it were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't drink with them, this brandy, because I don't drink alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand. What I said was it was a rather informal group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There was not anybody in charge of this thing, was there? There was not anybody that you could sit there and say: "This guy is in charge of this group"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that there was anybody in charge and I never followed anybody in my own life, and nobody could talk me into doing any of these things. I can blame mostly my mother for having done this and engaging in this kind of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, I think your mother probably was like my mother for telling her sons what to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think it is probable, sir. Your group did not wear any uniforms, did they, that group in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any uniforms. Maybe there were some uniforms, old ones from the JNA, which we had been issued as military conscripts of the JNA, under which oath we were, and I am still actually under their oath. I still haven't broken off my contract with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you have done your national service then, your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did my military service as a conscript of the JNA and I had an obligation to respond to any calls from them, and then you could have sanctions if -- I could have even been put in jail had I not responded to the calls, and some people who were there could tell you about that. We were under oath as long as we were military age, and as long as we were able to carry arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On May 19th your village was attacked; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date, but approximately -- I don't know if it was 19th or 20th. One of those. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor said the 19th, that would be about right, would it not, give or take a few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Give or take a couple of days. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Basically what occurred was there was some shelling of the village and a couple of people were killed by the shelling, and then your father arranged a surrender; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't my father who arranged for the surrender. He talked on the telephone together with another man, with the President of the Municipality, and he told them that the shelling would stop, that the military age men should get their weapons and should start going towards Celebici, and that they would be met by the TO and the HVO police, and then they would be sent back home when these formalities about the surrender of the weapons were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So there were about 20 armed men against 1,000 attacking the village. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how many people in the village were armed and who could defend the village, but I know that they did not defend the village, and I also don't know on the other side how many people did attack. I could not really count the people who attacked the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when you said in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor: "There were about 20 of us against over 1,000 attackers", that was just your best guess; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how we felt, which can be seen based on the fact that we didn't -- maybe this was my impression of the firing, and you said a moment ago 4,000. I don't think there were 4,000. I don't think they could have that many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did I say that, sir? If I said 4,000 I apologise. I wanted to say 1,000. About 10 of you slipped away and did not surrender that day, about 10 armed men; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our village at Cerici and Donje Selo together there were about 10 men total that did not surrender on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And Milovan Kuljanin was one of them, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Milovan Kuljanin was one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, did he have a firearm? Did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milovan Kuljanin did have a firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What did he have, sir? Do you recall what type of weapon it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a handgun, which he turned in, and he had a small-calibre rifle with a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A sniper scope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a small-calibre rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me jump ahead a little bit to when you got to the camp, when you got to Celebici; okay? When you got there, was there any organisation to the camp or was it like a madhouse over there, with nobody in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that it was worse than a madhouse. I never had an opportunity to be in a madhouse, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There was not any organisation at all to the place, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that people could go about in an organised way doing this to people that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And on that first interrogation you had, that was Mr. Zovko, was it not, nicknamed Kuhar, K-U-H-A-R?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's my childhood friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now he is a police officer, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was an investigator in the Ministry of the Interior in Konjic. I don't know what he does now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He was a lawyer also, was he not, an advocate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't know that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And he wrote down what you said and made a record of his interrogation, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you get to see that record of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I was a bit excited then and a bit scared, but I may have seen the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fair enough. If you do not recall, you do not recall. He put you in a category of the most dangerous type of prisoner; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was. It was strange to me, and I was disappointed about Mr. Zovko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now you were at the interrogation and I was not. I am just going to ask you about your feeling about this. If you do not know and cannot answer, that is fair enough. Did you get the impression that the fact you were captured with a machine gun, a fully automatic weapon, might have had something to do with him considering you to be one of the more dangerous prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would have to ask him about that. I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fair enough, a fair enough answer. Now, you had been held in that manhole way at the back of the camp for a couple of hours before that interrogation; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then after that interrogation you were moved to Tunnel 9; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that interrogation I was moved to prison hospital Number 22, where I was until 1 o'clock after midnight, when I was taken out by -- when I was taken to Sevko Niksic and Jasmin Guska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That was the second interrogation; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the second interrogation, but without keeping a record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sevko Niksic and Guska, and there were some other people there, were there not? They were all from the MUP, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Also Narcis was present there. He was a Warrant Officer of the JNA, and Miralem and Niksic Sevko and Jasmin and there was a younger man, whom I did not know. I don't think he was from the MUP, and there was also Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Hazim was in and out; is that not right? He was not there the whole time. That is what you testified on direct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us talk a little bit about the MUP. I know you are not an expert on the MUP, but nobody has really discussed it, and I think it is probably as good a time as any. The MUP is the Ministry of the Interior; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the MUP includes the secret police, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Before the break-up of Yugoslavia, there was a secret police, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware there was a secret police. I might give you an answer that might even offend you, but if I knew about it, then it would not be a secret police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, that is true. Sir, first, no truthful answer is going to offend me, but there were investigators and a part of the MUP that investigated special types of crimes or crimes against the state like espionage, sabotage, treason, things like that, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't quite understand the point of your question. I like to talk to you, but I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, for instance, in my country this group would be called the Federal Bureau of Investigation. In Mr. Greaves's country, it would be called the Special Branch?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object, it has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or perhaps it could have been called State Security in your country. In any case --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was State Security. That I am familiar with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was that part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't know why we are talking about this. I am a mechanic by trade and I can talk about the things I know about, not about MUPs and state security services. These are things that I do not know. I may give an answer which may not be qualified, and then I will be put to shame in front of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, that would be the last thing I would want to do. What I am getting at is: did some of these police agencies and police organisations, be it the ordinary police or criminal investigators, or people like that, have a reputation for perhaps in interrogations using physical means of getting answers? I am dancing around and basically I am asking you, whether or not they actually did, did they have the reputation of beating confessions out of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never beaten by anyone until I was taken to Celebici. They didn't have courage to beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But when you got there and Sevko Niksic and Jasmin Guska and the others were there, they did beat you, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They burnt me. I said that they burnt me with red hot scissors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then the young -- then there was a beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten by Bato Alikadic and occasionally some other people would join in that I couldn't see really, because it's not so easy to watch and to see who is hitting you, when ten people are hitting you from all sides at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. That is fair enough. When the beating was over with and you regained your consciousness, Mr. Delic took you to the bathroom and helped you clean up, let you clean up, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time, and he told me: "Hurry up. They'll kill you, you see." At least, that is what I understood, that I should hurry up and wash as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Who were the "they" that were going to kill you? Did he tell you? Was it the MUP people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably these people who had been burning me, who were mistreating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He was doing what he could to get you away from those people that he said were threatening to kill you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me to wash and he took me to Tunnel Number 9. That's all he did for me that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And a couple of days later some other people took you out of Tunnel Number 9, did they not, Bato -- I will spell his last name -- A-L-I-K-A-D-I-C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken out by the guards and they took me to Bato Alkadic and the others, whose name I listed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And again these people were trying to beat you to get information about some other weapons, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't want to beat me up. They did beat me up in order to get information about the hunting weapons of my father, which was buried, and for which he had regular licence for 30 years, and they also asked me some other questions that I couldn't answer. I was even asked questions about my private life by Mr. Alkadic, Bato Alkadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He was part of MUP, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't admit him. He wasn't there until the war started. I am afraid, I think, some things are not clear to you. Anybody could be anything, a captain and a general. For instance, this Narcis who burnt me, I know he was a Warrant Officer and Dusko called him "Captain". So, you know, he was promoted very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true. I understand. After those people beat you, you were put down in the manhole behind Tunnel 9; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were down there not very long before someone took you out; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was there for a couple of hours. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You asked to be let out then, and the person that was talking to you said that he could not let you leave then right now, because those people were still around. Is that not basically what he said: "They are still here. I can't let you go now"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is right, but I do not know who he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Were there any other people who were not normally around the camp besides Bato and his friends, his colleagues that you had seen earlier in the day or that you had seen when you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I saw Bato and these others, whose names I gave, but I don't know whether there were any others. Maybe there were, but this was 1 o'clock, after midnight. I could not see all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right. It was very dark. I understand, sir. A few hours later you were then released from the manhole and returned to, what, Tunnel Number 9 at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And a few days later -- was it about one or two days later -- Pavo Mucic and Hazim Delic brought you out of Tunnel 9 and asked you what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And at that point you were taken to Building 22, which is the medical facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day, but a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you received what medical care was available? Is that true: you received whatever medical care was available for your injuries in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They just tried to treat my ear, nothing else, because they didn't have anything. They gave me some drops for my ears and I had no other medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, that was because that is all they had, is that not right? All the doctors had to treat you with was what they had. Is that fair, a fair assessment? Is that a fair statement of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they had some medicines -- if they had some medicines, and as they were Serb doctors, they wouldn't have let me die, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you received the best medical care that was available at the camp at the time? Is that a fair statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you among all the injuries that doctors can treat, all I used were eardrops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And at some point about this time your father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I think let us rise for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, may I remind you that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir. A few quick questions and I think we are probably going to be done. Let me jump back to Guska Jasmin. Did anyone from MUP or maybe even Mr. Jasmin himself accuse you of making threats to kill him, to kill Mr. Jasmin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he mentioned it somewhere, but he didn't mention it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Pero Mrkajic, do you know about him, about his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know that that man died in the camp, but he was never in contact with me during my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On your direct examination you said that on at least one occasion Mr. Delic gave you some bacon or some ham to eat. That is not the only time he gave you food, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only time was when he gave me this bacon and a couple of times he gave me a cigarette to light.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He never gave you a beer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Once, I just remembered, Mr. Delic came into Number 9, after I had been beaten up and burnt, and he brought some brandy in a bottle, and he offered me to take a sip, and as I didn't because I don't drink, then he told me to use it to wash my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was after the people from MUP beat you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: After you were released, did you have any other contact with Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Delic in Donje Selo once. I think I and Dragan Sinikovic were putting a windshield on his car, Sastava 750.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you worked on his car after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not working on his car, but we were helping him to change the glass. I happened to be there by chance and I helped them do it, because it had been broken obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A couple of other quick questions. In Building 22, the hospital facility, the windows in that building, were those windows clear glass like the glass behind you, or was it glass that you could not see through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly it was glass that you couldn't see through, but the window could be opened up to a quarter. It couldn't be opened entirely, but it could be folded, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when the window was closed, you could not see out the windows; is that right? When the window was closed, it was impossible to see out of the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the chance to look through that window a couple of times, and it was open then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When it was closed, you could not see through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I watched once when some prisoners were being bathed with a hose, and the second time was when I saw this incident with Mr. Susic, but I never even looked through those windows. There may have been a pane that you could see through and others that you couldn't, but I can't recollect exactly now. I had worse problems. I couldn't clean and look through windows all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, sir. The job you had outside, cleaning up around the area, that was fairly light work, was it not? It was picking up cigarette butts, pieces of paper, that kind of thing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes I would push the garbage can out, but it wasn't hard work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, that job was kind of a special privilege, because it gave you more time outside in the fresh air; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't like to go out really, because whenever you went out, you were exposed to the danger of being beaten, so it wasn't an advantage. For some people it might have been an advantage, but for me I didn't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, the two hunting rifles that your father had -- it was two, was it not, hunting rifles that your father had hidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My father had on his licences for weapons two hunting rifles -- three -- two hunting rifles, one small-calibre rifle and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And those hunting rifles, they had telescopic sights, scopes on them, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And about the time you were arrested, the MUP had two of its people killed by a sniper, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of that. When I was arrested, two people were killed with sniper fire? I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: About the time that you and your father were taken into custody. If you do not know about it, that is just fine. Did the people from MUP ever accuse you or your father, to your knowledge, of being involved with being snipers and shooting two MUP members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. My father and me were both hunters and, of course, it was normal for us to use those weapons while hunting. We didn't use them for killing people. Such a thought never occurred to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, I am not accusing you of doing it. I am just saying did MUP accuse you of doing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they did, then that is their affair. They must have proof for such things and probably they wouldn't have let me go if they believed I had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, last question: you testified on direct examination that at some point Mr. Mucic told you that getting you out of the camp may not have helped you much, because you could get killed by anyone; remember when you testified to that on direct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember, yes, that is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you that, sir, or did he tell you, as you recount in your statement, because the men from MUP or others could come and kill you more easily at home than in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said men from MUP. That may be an error in the translation. It could have been men from MUP or anybody else who could come home and kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, have you talked about your testimony here with anyone except Ms. McHenry, what you were going to go testify to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone before you came to The Hague about what your testimony was going to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is Mr. Mucic's turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honour. Mr. Golubovic, I represent Pavo Mucic in this case, and I am going to ask you some questions, if I may, upon his behalf. If you do not understand my question, do not be shy. You tell me straight away and get me to repeat it or make it a better question; all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, I want to ask you, first of all -- you have told us a little bit about how well you knew Pavo Mucic before the war, but can we just put a little bit more detail into that, if we may? You have told us that he was friendly with, I think, a relative of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not want to know the relative's name, but how close a relative to you was that? Cousin or brother, or what? Is that something which distresses you, Mr. Golubovic? I will not pursue the matter, if that is the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that we offer, with your Honour's permission, the witness just a five-minute break if he would like it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help me about this, Mr. Golubovic: for how long before the war had you known Pavo Mucic through that relative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him some ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you meet him other than through the relative that you have talked about, in other places apart from with that relative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we never met. I would see him driving by. We would say: "Hello." I don't know whether we talked altogether twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You have told the court that you were not really friends and you would not describe your relationship as one of friendship, merely of acquaintance. Is that a fair description, simply someone you knew as an acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We somehow didn't look very kindly upon each other actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my next question. The reality was that you did not really like him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I will come towards the end of my questioning to how you feel about him now, but perhaps we can just move on to some of the events which led you to change your attitude towards him. I want to ask you a little bit about the incident where you were put down the manhole, Mr. Golubovic, and ask you some questions about that. When you were brought out and you saw Pavo Mucic outside -- I think you have described it as being on a wooden bed -- you have told us that he indicated to you that he would like to release you from the manhole, because you did not have enough air, but that he was not able to do so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. He said that he was going to go and request some people to question me, so that he could release me from the manhole. Simply put, to intervene on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So he had to go and get permission from somebody else before he could do that; that is what he was saying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that he had to see that they didn't have people there who -- since in the certificate from the HVO it stated that I had to be put in a separate room, so I had to stay in the manhole and that he could not take me out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was not his decision, and he had no control over that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably so, since he was not able to let me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think it is right that at that point he was able to persuade those who were also there to give you some water. Do you remember that? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, because we did get water.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me about this, please, Mr. Golubovic. It was then during the night that policemen from Konjic, MUP policemen, arrived at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I did not end it with a question and I am sorry. It is right, is it not, that that night Pavo Mucic was not in the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see Pavo Mucic at the camp that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as you knew, he never slept there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know. Maybe he even did, but I didn't see his vehicle very frequently. When I was in Number 22, I could see his vehicle parked in front, but I never saw him at night or sleeping there or coming into the camp. He never even entered into this infirmary during the night, so it is most probable that he didn't sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it not the case that you, when you were aware that he was in the camp, you and your fellow prisoners knew that you could sleep peacefully and have proper rest; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the feeling that I had. I cannot speak for others, because everybody has to say what their opinion is, but my feeling was that Mr. Mucic was there, I felt fairly secure, more so than when he was not around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On the day after you were assaulted by MUP policemen he came to see you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And he wanted to know what had happened to you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, I am about to ask you about whether you had the courage to tell him or not. It is not a reflection on your bravery, you will understand, but I want to ask you this: you did not have the courage to tell him what had happened to you, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have the courage to tell him, because he was maybe asking me -- I didn't know what his intentions were, but if I told him, then he would tell them, and then they would come back and mistreat me again, and so that's why I didn't tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he would try and find out anyway, even if you wouldn't tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When MUP had left the night before, had they threatened to come back again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. They said that they would come back in 24 hours, but they did not come back in 24 hours. They only arrived at the following day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was then, I think, that the incident with the bullets, the pistol being fired, that is when that took place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly what incident you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think a man called Bato Alkadic assaulted you, having ordered you to kneel down and kicked you with his boots; is that right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And on that occasion fired some bullets from his pistol close to your head? ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as you know, Pavo Mucic was not in the camp that night either, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And, indeed, you did not see him for several days after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him three, four -- no, two, three days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I think that when you next saw him, you were busy washing your face; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We were going out to wash up. There was a faucet there towards the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When he spoke to you, I think you were perhaps hobbling a bit, unable to walk perfectly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
