utterances.text: That is correct, because my pelvis was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He wanted to know what had happened to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We discussed that just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again you felt unable to tell him, because you were still uncertain as to what his attitude was going to be and what his role was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want just to deal now with some incidents that happened during the time that you were in the camp, Mr. Golubovic, please. Can I ask you about this: did you on one occasion hear him speaking to the guards within the camp if the prisoners had been given some food on a particular occasion? I think this was when you were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard him, yes, correct. This was when Mr. Mucic -- I heard his voice on that occasion and he asked: "Did you give them food?" They said: "No." He said: "Let the guard not get any food but give these people in the infirmary food right away."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the guard, I think, replied something along the lines of: "They have not been given food, because it has been impossible to get food from the town due to shelling and war activity." That is a summary of what was said. Can you just perhaps confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall now. There was always some conversation in front of the door, so I did not register everything, but I think that maybe on one occasion there was a talk about how the food could not be delivered because of the shelling of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic said something along these lines, did he not: "It may be the guards do not get any food, but the sick people and the people in the camp should get food, whatever the difficulties." Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you were then in the hospital and after that you were largely left alone or completely left alone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct and I stated that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Mucic when you were in the hospital on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he would come to the infirmary, he would sort of make jokes and sometimes he would bring some medicine. Then he would bring some fresh clothes to the doctors. Maybe we did speak, but there was nothing of importance so that I would remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was not going to suggest anything of importance, simply that he would come and pass the time of day with you. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would usually when he would come, he would, you know, smile at me or wink at me, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from the occasion you have described, when he shared some roast meat with you, would you accept that on occasions he also brought food to you in the hospital, and indeed his food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember on one occasion there was some food. I think there may have been some cakes. I don't know if it was his food, but he did bring it and give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that you had some skills as a car mechanic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I think on occasions he asked you if you would do some work on his car; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes I did, but mostly I would just pour gas with another guy, and on one occasion I was putting away his scuba-diving equipment and let it dry. I never was doing any hard physical labour and was not asked to do that either by Mr. Mucic or by the other guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you was this: on those occasions when you were doing something in relation to the car, it is right, is it not, that he gave you some cans of food or a can of food; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he gave me two tins with fish. He gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And some cigarettes on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already stated that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You will have to forgive me for going over old ground, Mr. Golubovic, but you will understand that it is important to the case I am putting before the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I said it once, I just thought that it was unnecessary to re-state it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I stand criticised, Mr. Golubovic; all right? On those occasions when he gave you either food or cigarettes, did he sometimes also say he wished he could give you some bread instead of what he was giving you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was saying that in reference to the cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this: on the occasions when you saw him in the area of the camp, would he sometimes wear civilian clothes when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him a number of times wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And sometimes he would be wearing military-style clothes but without insignia of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. He had a camouflage shirt and he had boots and pants. He had a pistol on his belt, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But no badges of rank and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he had no insignia and no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from the car that he had and that you did some bits and pieces for, was there also a motorcycle that you saw him using?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He did come on his motorcycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this, please? Was there an occasion when he was speaking to you and said something along these lines, that he would try to protect you as far as he could, but he could not do that in relation to MUP, and he had no control over MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the reason for that was MUP were a law unto themselves and had free run of the place, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that they could come whenever they want and get in there and they would not need to report to anyone, and to do these searches and questionings and that they didn't have to account to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the incident involving you being beaten over these hunting rifles, Mr. Golubovic. You have told the court that both you and your father were hunting people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just explain this to you: I am also someone whose father was a hunting person and I go hunting and I hope my son will follow me afterwards, so I understand about these things. Hunting rifles are very important to hunting people, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. My grandfather was a hunter, my father was and so am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And hunting people look after their weapons with great care and great love, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how it should be, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is exactly how it should be, and no doubt they had been buried with that in mind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The hunting rifles had been buried somewhere. Is that what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The rifles were buried -- but I didn't know where they were buried; only my father knew that -- two months before the attack to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: MUP had obviously found out about the existence of these rifles, and that is why they were very anxious to know where they were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rifles were properly registered, so they could find that in their files, and my father was known by everyone. Everybody knew that he was a hunter. So it would not have been a problem to find that out about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What Mr. Mucic was trying to do was to persuade you to tell them where the rifles were in order to get the beatings to stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. He told my father if the rifles were more important than someone's lives, and that people were getting beaten up for that, because apparently my father had told him that the rifles had been stolen. So he didn't want to part with them. He had given the small-calibre rifle to Midhat Pirkic, but he wanted to keep those too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This was because it was MUP who were beating you up, over whom he had no control; is that not it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Similarly some good advice was given to you, and -- sorry to go repeating this -- good advice was given to you about not going anywhere near the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I also mentioned that and there is no need for me to repeat it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you just about one thing, if I may. Would your Honour just give me a moment, please, because I have lost it in my notes? (Pause). I think you know the name Petko Grubac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember that he did something on behalf of Petko Grubac on occasions, helped him get some new clothes and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that he brought him some iron shirts and some cakes, and I think that Petko's wife had brought that, but he spoke to him much more than he did to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What are "iron shirts"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think he means shirts that had been ironed, so "freshly ironed" is how I interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It says "iron", not "ironed." I was just wondering: was he bringing some armour or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, I want to turn now, if I may, to the circumstances in which you were released from the camp, and the date, I think, was 17th July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You went into the camp kitchen and you found a guard eating in the camp kitchen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Mucic was sitting there and eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it the case that he told you to go to the van but did it quietly and discreetly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nevertheless you went to the car and found there Slovko Golubovic, that is your father, the huntsman, and your cousin, Milovan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you got in the car and you asked your father where you were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Pavo showed up five minutes later and you all drove away from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On the way on that journey is it right that you met a number of women who were returning from the camp and they had been taking some food to their relatives; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I already stated that a little while ago. Those were women -- those women were Gosa Cecez, Radojka Suka and several other. Maybe five or six of them. I can't recall all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You thought at that stage that you were going to the sports hall at Musala; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father told me that he thinks -- when I asked him where are we going, he said: "Most likely we are going to the sports hall."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But, in fact, it was to -- in front of your own home in Donje Selo that you went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And not only did he give you your release paper, but I think your father and cousin also got theirs at the same time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not my brother, but my father and my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think I only mentioned your father and cousin, but if I mentioned brother, then I didn't mean to. Sorry, Mr. Golubovic. It was then that you had the conversation with him, was it not, that he was not sure that he had done the right thing for you, and that you might actually be in more danger at home than you would be in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- I understand that sometimes you have to repeat things to get to the -- sort of the new point you are making, but just in the interest of having a fair and expeditious trial, with all due respect, I must object to the repetitive questioning that is going on, although it is being done in -- not a harrassing manner, I believe. It is unnecessary and unnecessarily prolonging this trial and this witness' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sorry. I am being fair to counsel. He is conducting his case in a way that is bringing some effect to his questioning. You do not have to object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This leads me to the next point, Mr. Golubovic. It is now this: that it was at this time that you began to change your attitude towards Mr. Mucic; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You began to realise that there was a different side to the man that you had known before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was at that time that you began to realise that you probably owed your life and your family members owed their lives to Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about your question, what you mean by it, but I could make it very short to say that I am very thankful to Mr. Pavo Mucic for releasing me and that he got involved and made an effort to find people who would take me to the Serb-held territory, and I don't think I would be sitting here had it not been for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Concerning the day of your release, was anybody else, apart from you and your father and cousin, released that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know on that day, but to our village only the three of us were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The vehicle that you were taken in from Celebici to Donje Selo, was sort of vehicle was it? A van or a truck or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a van of Iveco make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was Pavo Mucic the only person in the van or was there a driver or anybody else with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a young man who drove the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you got to your home village were there some photographs taken on a video recorder of some sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went there, nothing was videotaped, but I was in the village when another group of prisoners arrived and Mucic did tape with his video camera at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long after you had gone home was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? Did you have any conversation on that day when the video was taken about Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What did he say about the prisoners who were being released? Did he say anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember what he told me about those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did he say anything as to why you were -- why he was photographing them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he thought I minded why he was doing that, because those people were in terribly poor shape, and he said to me: "Golub, this tape may perhaps save your life and mine."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You have told us that a number of prisoners were brought back ten days later. Were there other occasions when prisoners were brought back by Pavo Mucic to your village, apart from that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw those prisoners being brought back. I may remember a couple of names of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps if we show you the video, you will help us and try to remember who they are. Perhaps the video could be shown now by the technical people, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask what video it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think it is the one we have already seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the one that is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I believe so. We do not appear to be getting anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We missed it. Perhaps we can just replay it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Golubovic, would you like us to go through that slowly, so you can pick out people you know the names of? Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people on this tape were not released then, when I was there. I didn't see them at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Right. Even if you did not see that release taking place, can you identify the people on the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised a few people from Bradina that I met in the camp. I don't know their names exactly, but when I was in Donje Selo, when those people arrived, it was not any one of these people. They were different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Golubovic. As far as the people who were released to your village, would you accept that it was something in the region of about 100 people after you had been released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not just to my village, but this whole area, probably about between 80 and 100 people were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us about some names. Would Zarko Mrkajic be one of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Mrkajic and Sreten Zelenovic, a butcher from Bradina, they were released a little after me and they were immediately transferred to Ilidza and from there to Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nedeljko Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nedeljko Draganic was released with that group that was photographed, Ratko Cecez, Nenad Cecez, and if I could see the tape, I would be able to see all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Aleksandar Draganic, do you remember him being released and helped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksandar Draganic was not released then. He was released later. He was in the sports hall and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Radoslav Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that man. He must be someone from Bradina. I know him but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think he has a nickname Bato?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is true. He was released maybe about ten days after me. He was released to the hamlet of Kuljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Milorad Kuljanin, did we deal with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Milorad Kuljanin and Miro Kuljanin, who was wounded in the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of the 80 to 100 people being released to the area of your village, the surrounding villages and so on, were they all brought out by Pavo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about all those people. I can only say about those that I saw. They were brought in, and the rumour in the village was that it was Pavo who brought them. Miso Radoslav, but Milorad Kuljanin, I did not see him drive them in, but I know that he drove them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In all, how frequent were releases made? Can you help us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my release from the camp maybe some ten days later, then the releases were more frequent, at an accelerated pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were releases taking place up until your departure to Serb-held territory in November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Up to 13th November. After that I had no contact with my family and the village so I don't know what happened, so I can't talk about it because I wasn't there and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want just now to turn to that same period and ask you if, apart from occasions when people were being released, Pavo Mucic made visits to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to my village, when he came to my village, he came to see me. I didn't see him visiting my village without dropping in on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many times that you recall him visiting you in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So about once a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could put it that way, or maybe once in 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you see him at all with other residents of Donje Selo during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would call on some people. He would call on the mother and father, the mother of Nedeljko Draganic, in my village. In Donje Selo he would call on Zoran Cecez and I don't know about the others. He would also visit Radoslav Kuljanin, his mother and father, then Miro Kuljanin who was wounded in the leg and I don't know any more. I can't talk about something I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did people talk about Pavo Mucic in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course they talked about him. All the people he had helped, they were grateful and they talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did he give you help in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He brought medicine for my mother and some detergents and things like that. Occasionally he would bring cigarettes too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Food on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would bring flour. These things for hygiene, for washing, and that sort of thing. We were not in such a bad need of food at the time, so he didn't have to bring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On one of the visits that he made to you in the period between July and November it is right, is it not, that he said to you that he was trying to get as many people released as possible from Celebici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He always said that things would be resolved, that there were no problems, that we should stay, that we shouldn't abandon our homes, and he was always saying that we shouldn't leave, that we should stay on in the village and the worst was behind us, that the camp would be closed down, and that it should be forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But there came a change in his advice to you and things obviously got worse politically, so that he came and told you you should go away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that a moment ago in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And also because winter was coming up and it was going to be very hard for the people in Donje Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so the idea was formed to get you and as many of you to Serb territory as possible; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic proposed to me that I should go, but he said that there was no need for my father and mother to go, that it was better for them to stay. I don't know about the others, what his intentions were, whether he advised them to go or to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But an arrangement was made for you to leave the territory and so you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you were offered 300 Deutschemarks by the people who arranged to take you, one of whom was Pavo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo asked me whether these people were trustworthy. Pavo didn't take me. I was driven by Zjelko Likota, Rajko Tomic and Ivica Bekavac. They offered -- Rajko Tomic offered me 300 Marks. I said that I didn't need them, that I had money. Then he said: "Pavo told me to give it to you." Then I told Rajko that he should give that money to my father, because I didn't need it, but he didn't give that money to my father. What happened I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear of other occasions when Pavo had given money to people in dire need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did, but it would be better for those people to say. I have said what he gave to me. I wouldn't like to speak on anyone's behalf. I didn't see it, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You have met on some occasions since you escaped to Serb-held territory in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you met him since you escaped into Serb-held territory at all since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you have had contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said this postcard that he sent. That was all. I was never in touch with Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a man called Mirko Cecez. Do you remember that person and that person dying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two Mirko Cecez. One is alive and one is dead so I do not know whom you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is the one who died at Musala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't die in Musala. He was killed in Musala. He was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not want to argue with you about the phraseology, Mr. Golubovic, but in any event, that is the one we are talking about. Did you speak to Pavo Mucic about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe we talked while I was in the camp and at home, but after I escaped to Serb territory, we didn't talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, can I just refresh your memory? Did he not tell you what he wanted to do concerning the death of Mr. Mirko Cecez, that he wanted to become the Commander at Musala, to try to stop these things happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. I am coming to a close, Mr. Golubovic. We talked earlier about your attitude to him before the war. What do you think of Mr. Mucic now that we are here in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago or rather at the beginning that I was grateful to Mr. Mucic for helping me in all my troubles, helping me and my father and my mother, and I am grateful. I am saying all this in my own name and I don't know what else to say. I think that it is not the man and I do not have the opinion of him that I had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember saying this to the Office of the Prosecution: "If at least 20 per cent of the people in Bosnia were like Mucic, there would have been no war"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember. I remember that. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is a fair remark, is it not, Mr. Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I think that still. Maybe I am wrong but that is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other questioning?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was informed that we were going to break at 5.30 today. Would you prefer that we just go ahead or wait until Monday? That would be fine with me. I only have about seven minutes, and I would really prefer to do it all at one time instead of breaking it up, if that is okay with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in terms of scheduling, I just wanted to raise one issue with the court. Sunday is Serbian Orthodox Easter, and I understand that there is a possibility that, although it is all uncertain, that the victim may have a chance to go to where he lives for the weekend to celebrate Easter with his family, since we are a little far behind, in which case he could be back Monday at 2.30. I also understand that we may have some legal arguments Monday morning. So if it works out, I am just finding out: would the court be willing to not resume this witness's testimony until 2.30 on Monday? . It may not be necessary. This has just come up recently but I wanted to raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is quite fine. We are having the information for the first time. We can afford to wait until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We will inform the court if, in fact, he decides to go and they can get a flight, etc. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I think we can adjourn. It is a pity we have to break for now, but it was inevitable we should do that. So we will resume again on Monday at 10 actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: --ooOoo--

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until Monday morning at 10 o'clock)
